hours.name: Mexican Canyon Trestle Vista (US-82) / Trestle Vista Observation Site
hours.when: Open year round, all hours — Forest Service lists the site status as Open with no season and no posted opening or closing time. Free. Parking is a pull-off directly off US-82 with approximately 10 spaces, also free. No restrooms, no potable water. The managing office, Sacramento Ranger District, 4 Lost Lodge Rd, Cloudcroft, is open Monday-Friday 09:00-15:00 — that is the OFFICE, not the vista.
hours.note: A second FS page, /recreation/mexican-canyon-trestle-vista-us82, lists the pin as 32.964,-105.748; the observation-site page's map link gives 32.9642532,-105.7474681. Elevation is not published by the FS. No fee, no gate, so a pre-dawn or after-dark arrival is physically possible — whether it is permitted is not published.

hours.name: Trestle (Depot) Recreation Area, Lincoln National Forest
hours.when: Open spring, summer and fall — DAY USE ONLY, no camping. No opening or closing clock time is published. Fee $5 per vehicle per day, or a New Mexico Enchantment Pass. Vault toilets and picnic tables; no potable water. Pets permitted, leashed at all times, clean up after them.
hours.note: FS map pin 32.957241,-105.748959. 'Day use only' with no published hours is the exact ambiguity that matters for a blue-hour shot — worth asking the district office.

hours.name: Sacramento Mountains Museum & Pioneer Village
hours.when: PROBABLY CLOSED FOR THIS STOP. Regular hours are winter (weather permitting) 10:00-16:00 Friday and Saturday, and summer from Memorial Day 10:00-16:00 Wednesday to Saturday; closed Sunday, Monday, Tuesday. Admission adults $5.00, children 6-12 $3.00, $1.00 discount per person for military with valid ID. But the museum shuts every autumn to build its Haunted Village: its own homepage carried 'We will be closed the month of September 2025 to prepare for Haunted Village', and its events page for the 13th annual event says 'We will be closed from Sept 2 to October 11 to prepare'. That is a recurring annual pattern, not a one-off, and it covers the whole of a late-September stay.
hours.note: 1000 Highway 82, Cloudcroft NM 88317, directly across from the Chamber. This should be a CALLS.md item: confirm the 2027 closure window before building a day around it, because 'closed Sept 2 - Oct 11' would remove the museum from the card entirely. Email smhsmuseum@yahoo.com.

hours.name: The Lodge Golf Course, Cloudcroft (nine holes, 1899)
hours.when: Nine holes, established 1899, played from different tees with separate flags to make 18 in the Scottish tradition; 4,858 yards men's, 4,319 yards ladies. Described by the operator as the 5th highest course in the US and 7th highest in the world, at about 9,000 ft. Tee times booked online through the-lodge-golf-course.book.teeitup.com. Limited carts for rent — availability must be confirmed by phone. Dress code enforced: collared shirt, tailored trousers or shorts, golf or soft-soled shoes. Daily opening and closing clock times and green fees are NOT published.
hours.note: thelodgeresort.com now 301-redirects to 223collectionhotels.com — the property has changed branding, so any older Lodge URL on the card is stale. Green fees, cart fee and first/last tee time are unpublished: phone.

hours.name: Cloudcroft Light Opera Company (CLOC)
hours.when: NOTHING IS PUBLISHED. The company's own Upcoming Events page reads 'Details on our upcoming events are coming soon!' and lists no performance, no date, no venue, no ticket price and no season. The site gives no telephone number. It is an all-volunteer 501(c)(3) putting on family-oriented theatre for Cloudcroft, the Sacramento Mountains and the Tularosa Basin.
hours.phone: no number published by CLOC — route the question through the Cloudcroft Chamber of Commerce, 575-682-2733
hours.note: Also on Facebook and Instagram as @CloudcroftLightOperaCo, where schedules appear to be announced in practice. Recorded as unknown rather than guessed; a 2027 schedule will not exist until well into 2027 in any case, so this is a call to make close to departure, not now.

hours.name: White Sands National Park
hours.when: PARK: open daily year round except Thanksgiving and Christmas. Gates open 07:00; the park closes 30 MINUTES AFTER LOCAL SUNSET, and NPS states local sunset runs 8 minutes earlier than Alamogordo's predicted sunset. The 1-hour-after-sunset extension is a summer exception covering 22 May - 7 Sep only, so a late-September visit gets the 30-minute rule. VISITOR CENTER: 09:00-17:00 daily, year round, closed Thanksgiving and Christmas; dogs not admitted (federal building). FEES: $25 per vehicle, $15 per person on foot or bicycle, $20 motorcycle, $45 White Sands annual, each valid seven consecutive days; America the Beautiful accepted. PETS: leashed, six-foot maximum, throughout the park. SUNSET STROLL: ranger-guided, Friday/Saturday/Sunday as staffing and weather allow, start time varies 16:00-19:00 by season and is timed to END at sunset, 45-60 minutes, meets at the sunset-stroll sign parking area 8 miles from the fee station, free with entry, no reservations taken; non-disruptive leashed pets welcome. FULL MOON NIGHT: monthly on the full moon, May-October, with extended hours; Moonlight Hike the night before each full moon, March-December.
hours.phone: 575-479-6124 (park); ext. 236 for programme status; 575-678-1178 (White Sands Missile Range, for US-70)
hours.note: MISSILE CLOSURES — the closure schedule IS published, as a dated table on the park's own page https://www.nps.gov/whsa/planyourvisit/park-closures.htm, and NPS asks visitors on a tight schedule to check it the day before arrival. Dunes Drive closes for up to three hours; US-70 between Alamogordo and Las Cruces closes with it, which also cuts the drive home. WSMR notice to the park may be as little as 24 hours. Unexpected weather closures go out, in NPS's stated order of priority, to the park's Facebook page and then NM DOT road conditions. FOR THIS STOP: computed full moons are 16 Sep and 15 Oct 2027, so a 25-30 Sep stay MISSES the Full Moon Night programme in both months — the compensation is that it lands on the new moon (30 Sep) for the astro shot.

hours.name: Apache Point Observatory / Sunspot Solar Observatory Visitor Center
hours.when: APACHE POINT: the grounds are open to the public DURING DAYLIGHT HOURS ONLY and it is not possible to go inside the buildings — the observatory states its site staff is too small. It 'occasionally offers site open houses', but no schedule is published. No admission, no tour, no night access. SUNSPOT VISITOR CENTER, 18 miles south of Cloudcroft at the end of the Sunspot Scenic Byway (NM-6563): sunspot.solar states 9:00-17:00 daily during peak season, with the Dunn Solar Telescope observation room open only on select days and callers told to ring for current times and the tour schedule. CONTRADICTION ON RECORD: the Forest Service page lists the visitor centre status as 'Open', while Apache Point's own visitor page says that as of early 2026 the Sunspot visitor centre is temporarily closed. Late-September status therefore unknown — phone before driving 36 miles round trip.
hours.phone: 575-434-7190 (Sunspot Visitor Center, published on sunspot.solar); 575-437-6822 supplied in the brief for Apache Point — NOT verified against apo.nmsu.edu, which publishes no number on its visiting page
hours.note: The 'daylight hours only' rule is the load-bearing fact and it kills the obvious idea of shooting the night sky from the observatory grounds. No restrooms and no potable water at the FS Sunspot site. Make this a CALLS.md item.

hours.name: The village itself — shops and restaurants, shoulder season
hours.when: UNKNOWN AND NOT PUBLISHED. No authority — Chamber, Village or otherwise — publishes consolidated shoulder-season trading hours for Burro Avenue. Two fixed points that ARE published: the Village Office is Monday-Friday 08:00-16:30, and the Chamber of Commerce answers on 575-682-2733. The Chamber's own event calendar shows nothing at all between the Labor Day Hoopla and Heritage Day Car Show (5-6 September, Zenith Park) and the Christmas Market in late November, which is consistent with a genuine shoulder week but is not a statement about trading hours.
hours.note: STALE URL WARNING for the card: villageofcloudcroftnm.net now 301-redirects to an unrelated third-party domain and must not be linked. The working village site is cloudcroftvillage.com. Expect individual restaurants to be closed one or two weekdays midweek in shoulder season — that is the pattern in mountain villages generally, not a sourced fact about Cloudcroft, and is recorded here as an assumption to check, not a finding.

hours.name: Seasonal events in late September (Oktoberfest, Aspencade, Aspenfest, Haunted Village)
hours.when: CLOUDCROFT OKTOBERFEST — the one that can land inside the stay. Hosted by Cloudcroft Brewing Company, 1301 Burro Avenue, not by the Chamber, and the dates MOVE: the brewery's own listing ran it Friday-Sunday 4-6 October one year, while a New Mexico statewide Oktoberfest round-up put Cloudcroft's on Saturday 27 September in 2025. Typically live music Friday evening, brat plates from noon Saturday and Sunday, and a best-dressed Trachten contest. ASPENCADE TOURS — mid-October, previously advertised as meeting 09:00 at the Cloudcroft Chamber over a weekend around 17-18 October; after a late-September stay. ASPENFEST is RUIDOSO's event, not Cloudcroft's, first Saturday in October, about 45 minutes north. HAUNTED VILLAGE — October, at the Sacramento Mountains Museum, and the reason the museum shuts from early September. LABOR DAY HOOPLA & HERITAGE DAY CAR SHOW — 5-6 September, Zenith Park; before a late-September arrival. The Chamber calendar currently lists NO event between early September and late November.
hours.open_in_late_september: unknown — Oktoberfest may or may not fall inside the stay
hours.phone: 575-682-2733 (Chamber); Cloudcroft Brewing Company is the operator for Oktoberfest
hours.note: THIS IS A CAMPGROUND-AVAILABILITY QUESTION, not just an activity. A last-weekend-of-September Oktoberfest in a village this small fills beds and sites and puts traffic on Burro Avenue; if the 2027 date lands inside the five nights, either book early or shift the window. No 2027 date is published by anyone yet — put it on the list to re-check in 2027.

hours.name: High Rolls, 20 minutes down US 82
hours.when: Lincoln NF trails, no gate and no posted hours. Ride or walk it in the morning — the monsoon rule applies here as it does on the rim.

shots.title: The 1899 trestle from the US-82 vista, first light
shots.subject: Mexican Canyon Trestle — 323 ft long, 52 ft above the canyon floor, built 1899 for the Alamogordo & Sacramento Mountains Railroad (the 'Cloud Climbing Railroad', worked 1899-1947), listed on the National Register 7 May 1979, ref. 79001543. It is the last big standing trestle on the route and the single image the village is known by. Worth it because it is a 60-second walk from a free pull-off and needs no permit, no hike and no dog arrangement.
shots.vantage: Mexican Canyon Trestle Vista, pull-off on US-82 immediately NW of the village. Forest Service publishes the pin as 32.9642532,-105.7474681 (Trestle Vista Observation Site page, Lincoln NF); free, no gate, roughly ten spaces. The NRHP coordinate for the trestle itself is 32.9636,-105.7478 — from the vista pin that is ~60-80 m away on a bearing of roughly 200-240 deg, i.e. BELOW you and to the south-west. Park the truck here; the coach never comes up this pull-off. Access onto the trestle itself is prohibited — it is a registered historic site, and Komoot’s highlight for it says so explicitly. Every frame here is from below or from across the canyon.
shots.light: MORNING. The trestle lies west/south-west of and below the camera, and Mexican Canyon drains west toward the Tularosa Basin, so every square inch of sky behind the subject is western sky. Shoot 07:00-08:30. By 16:00-19:00 the sun has swung to az 240-270 deg, directly behind the subject: that is flare and a black lattice, which is a legitimate picture but not a picture of a trestle. If you want that version, take it in the last 20 minutes before sunset (~18:45) and expose for the sky.
shots.craft: 70-200 mm to compress the lattice and shoot over the highway furniture; f/8-f/11 so the near and far bents both resolve. What ruins it: the guardrail and roadside scrub in the bottom of the frame — the fix is focal length, not position, because there is nowhere else to stand. Second killer is hand-holding 200 mm in cold thin air at 07:00; brace on the rail or bring the tripod.
shots.season: Year round — US-82 is the main highway over the pass and is kept open. The stay is 22–29 Aug, inside that window — but late August is PEAK MONSOON here (5.65 in in August against 3.10 in September), so the binding constraint is the hour, not the date: mornings only, and out of canyons and washes before the afternoon.
needs: Vista elevation not published by the Forest Service (a third-party byway listing says 8,517 ft — not sourced from an authority, do not print it).
Whether the pull-off is signed and safely enterable for eastbound as well as westbound traffic — unverified.
Bearing vista-to-trestle is computed from two separately published pins ~70 m apart; treat as approximate.

shots.title: Last light on the gypsum, White Sands
shots.subject: The dunefield of White Sands National Park — the largest gypsum dune field on earth, an hour and 4,000 ft down the hill from the campground. The famous frame is low sun raking the ripples so the crests separate from the troughs. It is also the rare marquee landscape where the DOG IS LEGAL: NPS allows leashed pets (6 ft maximum) throughout, excluded only from the visitor center and other federal buildings.
shots.vantage: Deep dunefield off Dunes Drive, roughly 6-8 miles in from the fee station — past the point where the road surface turns to packed gypsum and the vegetation stops. NPS-published pins: visitor center 32.7796594,-106.1723908; the backcountry camping loop, in the heart of the dunes, 32.809869,-106.264225. The ranger Sunset Stroll meets at a signed parking area 8 miles from the fee station, which is a good proxy for where the dunes are deepest. Truck only; the coach stays in Cloudcroft.
shots.light: EVENING, and the gate is the constraint, not the light. Sun sets az ~270 deg — dead west, straight down the axis of the basin and into the San Andres Mountains, which is why this shot works here and not at 30 deg either side of the equinox. Golden hour from ~18:25; computed sunset ~19:03, and NPS states local sunset at the park runs 8 minutes earlier than Alamogordo's predicted sunset. So you get roughly 20-25 usable minutes after the sun goes and then you must be driving the 8 miles out. Plan the exit before you plan the frame. Blue hour proper (ends ~19:13) is the last thing you will get; astronomical dark at ~20:20 happens outside the gate.
shots.craft: 24-70 mm; f/11 with focus about a third into the nearest dune holds both the ripple texture and the range. What ruins it: your own footprints. Walk in on the leeward flank and shoot back across untracked crests, and check the frame edges before you press. Second killer: changing a lens in blowing gypsum — it is a mild abrasive and it gets into the mount.
shots.season: Open daily year round except Thanksgiving and Christmas. The live risk is a missile test: Dunes Drive closes for up to three hours and US-70 between Alamogordo and Las Cruces closes with it, on as little as 24 hours' notice. Check nps.gov/whsa/planyourvisit/park-closures.htm the day before, and build a spare evening into the five nights.
needs: No NPS coordinate published for the sunset-stroll sign parking area itself; the pin given is NPS's backcountry-loop pin in the same part of the dunefield.
Whether the backcountry loop trail is open for day use in 2027 (backcountry camping has been suspended in recent years) — 575-479-6124.

shots.title: Four thousand feet down — White Sands from the Osha rim
shots.subject: The western rim of the Osha Trail, looking straight down onto the Tularosa Basin. The Forest Service's own fact sheet for the trail says it 'offers stunning views of the Tularosa Basin which includes White Sands National Monument' (the sheet is dated April 2015 and predates the 2019 redesignation as a national park). This is the picture that explains the stop: the white sheet of gypsum lying 4,000 ft below a fir forest. 2.1 miles, 8,600 ft, graded easy-to-moderate by the FS, benches at the vistas — appropriate ground for a 53-year-old walker. Pets are explicitly allowed: 'Hikers, pets and pack animals only', leashed.
shots.vantage: Rim vistas on the western half of the Osha Trail loop. Main trailhead just west of Cloudcroft at the junction of US-82 and Muchachita Street, 'just down the road from the Mexican Canyon Trestle Vista', parking on site (Forest Service fact sheet, fs.usda.gov/media/94558). The Forest Service publishes no coordinate for this trailhead, so none is recorded here.
shots.light: TWO DIFFERENT PICTURES, and morning is the one most people get wrong. You are aimed WEST and DOWN. The gypsum only reads as a white sheet when it is frontlit, which means morning: 07:30-09:30, sun at az 95-110 deg behind your shoulder, and basin haze at its daily minimum before convection starts. In the evening the sun is at az 250-270 deg — behind and beyond the dunes — and the basin goes to contre-jour: you lose the white entirely but gain the San Andres as stacked blue ridges with the sun dropping into them, ~18:25-19:03. Pick one deliberately. If you take the evening version, you will finish a 2.1-mile loop at 8,600 ft in the dark: head torch, and the dog on a short lead.
shots.craft: 100-400 mm to lift the dunefield out of 30+ miles of basin; f/8. What ruins it is atmosphere — heat shimmer and dust across that distance turn the whole thing into a grey band, so shoot early or the morning after a front has been through. A 24 mm wide of this view is always disappointing; the subject is small and far away and needs the long end.
shots.season: FS: open all year, most used summer and fall. No water and no restrooms on the trail.
needs: No published coordinate for the Osha trailhead from the Forest Service.
Which of the rim benches has the clean line to the dunefield — not published; establish it on the first morning.
Trail time not published by the FS.

shots.title: Aspen gold on the Sunspot Byway
shots.subject: The aspen stands along NM-6563, the Sunspot Scenic Byway, which New Mexico Tourism describes as 'a 16-mile ribbon of asphalt, surrounded by aspens' running south from Cloudcroft along the Sacramento crest to the Sunspot and Apache Point observatories. Paved the whole way — a straightforward truck drive with the dog aboard.
shots.vantage: Pullouts along NM-6563 between Cloudcroft and the observatories, roughly 16-18 miles. From the village take NM-130 south then right onto NM-6563 (Forest Service directions for the Sunspot Solar Observatory Visitor Center at the byway's end). Neither the Forest Service nor New Mexico Tourism publishes coordinates for individual pullouts, so none is recorded.
shots.light: BACK- OR SIDE-LIT, which for a west-facing rim pullout means the last 90 minutes before sunset: ~17:30-19:00, sun az 250-270 deg, low enough to fire straight through the leaves and make them glow rather than merely look yellow. Overcast is the honourable alternative and saturates the gold better than blue sky does. The hour to avoid is 11:00-15:00, when the sun sits 46-56 deg up and flattens everything.
shots.craft: 35-85 mm; f/4-5.6 to lift white trunks off a gold background. The biggest single improvement is a polarizer used at ~90 deg to the sun — it strips the specular glare off the leaf surfaces and the colour deepens visibly. What ruins it is wind: aspen leaves are hinged to flutter in almost no air at all, so 1/250 s minimum even in still conditions, and abandon the shot in a real breeze.
shots.season: THE RISK ON THIS ONE IS THE DATE. New Mexico Tourism's own advice is that aspen colour 'is fleeting, lasting only about a week in most places' and to fix your travel dates in advance but not your destination. No agency publishes a peak-colour date for the Sacramento Mountains. Treat it as opportunistic, not scheduled. The stay is 22–29 Aug, inside that window — but late August is PEAK MONSOON here (5.65 in in August against 3.10 in September), so the binding constraint is the hour, not the date: mornings only, and out of canyons and washes before the afternoon.
needs: No authority publishes a fall-colour report or peak window for the Sacramento Mountains; Sacramento Ranger District 575-682-2551 is the number to ask on arrival.
No sourced coordinates for the best aspen pullouts.

shots.title: Milky Way over the Sacramento rim
shots.subject: Night sky from the ridge the observatories chose. Apache Point Observatory (home of the 3.5 m ARC telescope and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey telescope) and the Sunspot Solar Observatory both sit on this crest about 18 miles south of the village — the siting is the evidence for how dark and steady this air is, and it is better evidence than any brochure. THE CONSTRAINT MOST LISTS GET WRONG: Apache Point's own visitor page says the grounds are open to the public 'during daylight hours only' and buildings cannot be entered. You cannot shoot from the observatory after dark. The night shot happens from public roadside, not from the science.
shots.vantage: Public pullouts on NM-6563 south of the village, and the Mexican Canyon Trestle Vista at 32.9642532,-105.7474681, which is a free, ungated Forest Service pull-off with no posted closing time. Note the light-dome problem: Alamogordo lies WSW and 4,000 ft below, so a west-facing rim vantage puts a town glow exactly where the galactic core sits on a late-September evening. For the core, prefer a pullout with a clear south to south-east horizon; use the rim only if you want the basin lights as a deliberate foreground element. The Trestle Recreation Area is DAY USE ONLY and is not a night option.
shots.light: NEEDS A DARK MOON, and the arrival date is not fixed, so this shot is specified by requirement: a night with the moon under about 30% illuminated, or setting before astronomical dark. Computed for 2027 that means the back half of a late-September stay — full moon 16 Sep, then 33% on 25 Sep falling to 13% on 27 Sep, 2% on 29 Sep, and NEW MOON on 30 Sep. A 25-30 Sep stay therefore ends on three effectively moonless nights. Astronomical dark begins ~20:20 MDT. The galactic core is already in the south-west and setting by then, so the core window is roughly 20:20-21:30 and closes early; the fainter summer arch overhead runs later.
shots.craft: 14-24 mm at f/2.8 or faster, ISO 3200-6400, 10-15 s untracked — the 500 rule suggests 25 s at 20 mm but coma and star drift bite well before that. Focus manually on a bright star at live-view magnification and tape the ring. What ruins it: dew on the front element. At 8,600 ft the glass radiates to a clear sky and fogs within the hour — a lens warmer band, not a cloth, and check the front element between frames.
shots.season: Clear-sky dependent. The stay is 22–29 Aug, inside that window — but late August is PEAK MONSOON here (5.65 in in August against 3.10 in September), so the binding constraint is the hour, not the date: mornings only, and out of canyons and washes before the afternoon.
needs: No dark-sky designation could be sourced for Cloudcroft or the Sacramento Mountains — do not claim one on the card.
Whether overnight parking or after-dark occupancy is permitted at the Trestle Vista pull-off is not published; Sacramento Ranger District 575-682-2551.
No sourced coordinate for a south-facing pullout on NM-6563.

shots.title: Under the bents — the trestle from the Trestle Recreation Area
shots.subject: The counter-shot to the postcard: the trestle's timber bents from close range and below, rather than the whole span from the highway. The Forest Service day-use area sits on the canyon floor side of the structure with picnic tables, vault toilets and about a 10-space feel, and it is the only sanctioned way to be near the trestle rather than looking at it. Dogs allowed, leashed at all times. Worth the walk because the 1899 carpentry is the actual subject and it is unreadable at 200 mm from the highway.
shots.vantage: Trestle (Depot) Recreation Area, E Little Mexican Rd, Cloudcroft. Forest Service map pin 32.957241,-105.748959. Day use only — no camping. $5 per vehicle per day, or a New Mexico Enchantment Pass. Vault toilets, picnic tables, no potable water. Access onto the trestle itself is prohibited — it is a registered historic site, and Komoot’s highlight for it says so explicitly. Every frame here is from below or from across the canyon.
shots.light: From below the subject stands against sky, so this is a tonal problem, not a golden-hour one. Midday (sun 46-56 deg up, az 135-210 deg) actually gives the most detail in the weathered timber and the least blown sky if you keep the sun outside the frame — unusual for a landscape stop, useful when the mornings are already committed to the vista shot. The alternative is the last light and blue hour, timbers black against colour to the west; but see the note below, because the area is signed day use.
shots.craft: 16-35 mm from directly beneath a bent, shooting up the diagonals; f/8. What ruins it is a bare white sky behind dark timber — the frame has no midtones and no amount of recovery invents them, so shoot it with cloud in the sky or accept the graphic black-on-white version and commit to it.
shots.season: Day use only. The stay is 22–29 Aug, inside that window — but late August is PEAK MONSOON here (5.65 in in August against 3.10 in September), so the binding constraint is the hour, not the date: mornings only, and out of canyons and washes before the afternoon.
needs: No posted opening and closing clock times for the recreation area; 'day use only' is all the FS publishes. Sacramento Ranger District 575-682-2551.
Whether a trail actually reaches beneath the trestle from the recreation area, and its length, is not published by the Forest Service.
The canyon's westward drainage is inferred from the railroad's Alamogordo-to-Cloudcroft climb and the published elevations, not from a published map bearing.

campgrounds.name: Sugar Pines RV Park
campgrounds.hookups: Full hookups — water, sewer, 30 AMP electric only, free Wi-Fi. 16 sites.
campgrounds.season: Not published by the operator. Third-party listings describe it as open all year; confirm by phone.
campgrounds.reservations: By telephone to the park — 575-682-3375. Also listed on Hipcamp and RoverPass.
campgrounds.note: The only RV park inside the Village of Cloudcroft, 601 Columbine Boulevard, at about 8,400-9,000 ft, walking distance to the shops and the Trestle Recreation Area — the best of the options for a dog that wants a walk from the door. TWO THINGS TO SETTLE BY PHONE. (1) The operator publishes NO maximum RV length anywhere on its site; the Allstays directory lists 45 ft max, 16 sites, 4 pull-throughs, but that is third-party and must not be relied on for a 40 ft coach on a village street. (2) 30 AMP ONLY — no 50 amp service. For a 2005 40 ft coach that means one air conditioner at a time and careful load management; Also: maximum 4 persons per site, and check-ins after dark are not permitted.

campgrounds.name: Silver Springs RV Park and Trout Pond
campgrounds.hookups: Full hookups — water, sewer, Wi-Fi, with 20, 30 and 50 amp service by site class. Clubhouse, community fire pit, stocked one-acre rainbow trout pond.
campgrounds.season: Open all year (winter sites by phone). The RV-storage season pass runs 15 May - 30 September, which is the park's own definition of the main season.
campgrounds.reservations: Online through the park's Premier Campground booking link from silverspringsrv.com, or by phone.
campgrounds.note: 449 NM-244, about 5 miles from Cloudcroft at nearly 9,000 ft — on the Ruidoso road, so the NM-244 drive starts at the gate. THE LENGTH IS UNPUBLISHED and the third-party figures disagree badly: RVshare, Outdoorsy and GoCampingAmerica all say 38 RV sites, all back-in, rigs to 45 ft; AllBiz says 42 spaces to 60 ft. Do not book on either number — phone. Two operator rules that matter for this rig: EVERY SITE IS BACK-IN (no pull-throughs, so the truck has to be unhooked before the site), and each site is limited to one RV and one vehicle with an additional charge for extras — the towed pickup will either be the one vehicle or will cost extra. Pets welcome on leash, not left unattended, $100 cleaning fee for waste left behind, no pets in the clubhouse. Office closed Wednesdays.

campgrounds.name: Boot Hill RV Resort, Alamogordo
campgrounds.hookups: Full hookups, 20/30/50 amp, pull-throughs and back-ins, gated, laundry, showers, dog runs, movie room, exercise room.
campgrounds.season: Open all year. The park warns sites fill fast in winter and spring.
campgrounds.reservations: Call or text 575-888-7031 for availability and to reserve; office 575-439-6224, boothillrv@gmail.com. Also bookable through Good Sam.
campgrounds.note: 1 Dog Ranch Road, Alamogordo, at about 4,350 ft — this is the fallback that removes the US-82 climb from the itinerary entirely, at the cost of camping in the desert instead of the pines and driving up the hill each day (about 30 minutes). It is the only one of the three that is unambiguously a big-rig park: pull-throughs, 50 amp, gated, enclosed dog runs. BUT the operator publishes no maximum length either — AAA lists 32 sites, 80 ft max RV length, 16 pull-throughs, 50 full hookups, 20/30/50 amp; another directory lists pull-thrus at 32 x 83 ft. Confirm on the phone. Rates as published: standard $55 + tax nightly, deluxe covered $70, premium $85. ALTERNATIVE WORTH A CALL: Camp Rio (formerly Camp at Cloudcroft), 2180 Rio Penasco Road, Mayhill NM, 575-687-3715, camprionm.com — 6,500 ft, about 30 minutes east of Cloudcroft on the gentle side of US-82, full hookups with 30 and 50 amp, 50-amp PULL-THROUGHS, open year-round, pets on leash welcome. It publishes no maximum length either, but third-party listings describe 34 full-hookup sites with room for rigs to 75 ft. If Silver Springs turns out to be short, this is the next call.

aurora.bandNote: too far south to be worth planning around

elevation_note: Cloudcroft is 8,676 ft; the campgrounds on the mountain sit between about 8,400 and 9,000 ft. THE COACH: the problem is not sitting at altitude, it is getting there. US-82 from Alamogordo climbs about 4,300 ft in roughly 16-17 miles at a sustained ~6% grade with tight curves and New Mexico's only highway tunnel — RV forums are consistent that this is a hard pull up and a serious brake test down, and the tunnel's posted clearance is not something I could source, so it needs checking with NMDOT before committing a 13'6" coach. The gentle alternative is to arrive from the EAST on US-82 via Artesia and Mayhill, which is a long gradual climb rather than a wall; that also puts Camp Rio at Mayhill and 16 Springs on the way in. At 8,600 ft a naturally aspirated gas coach loses roughly 3% of power per 1,000 ft — about a quarter of its output — while a turbodiesel loses much less; either way plan the climb in low gear, watch coolant and transmission temperature, and descend on the engine brake rather than the service brakes. The generator will also derate and may need a jet/altitude adjustment for extended use, and propane appliances light less willingly. THE DOG: coming up from Alamogordo or the plains, the dog is gaining 4,000-5,000 ft in under an hour. Give it 24-48 hours before any long walk, keep water in front of it constantly, keep the first day's outings short and flat (the Trestle Recreation Area loop rather than the Osha rim), and watch for laboured breathing, unusual lethargy or refusal to eat — the same signs you would watch in yourself. the same applies to the cat's water. The upside is real: this is one of the coolest places in the Southwest in September, and every trail listed here except White Sands is dog-legal on a leash.

monsoon.season: The National Weather Service designates the Monsoon Season as 15 June - 30 September; NWS Albuquerque and NWS Tucson both use those dates. NWS ABQ puts average onset at 'around July 3 for the southwest corner of the state'. So 22-29 August is not near either end of the season - it is in the middle of it. The stay is 22–29 Aug, inside that window — but late August is PEAK MONSOON here (5.65 in in August against 3.10 in September), so the binding constraint is the hour, not the date: mornings only, and out of canyons and washes before the afternoon.
monsoon.late_august_position: PEAK, not the tail. Cloudcroft's own COOP record settles it: WRCC station 291931 (CLOUDCROFT, NM), period of record 01 Sep 1987 - 10 Jun 2016, 99.4% of possible observations, gives average total precipitation of Jul 5.96 in, Aug 5.65 in, Sep 3.10 in, against an annual 29.58 in. July and August alone are 11.61 in - 39% of the year's rain in two months. August is 82% wetter than September. The stop has been moved from the drying-out side of the monsoon onto the wettest fortnight of the Cloudcroft year. NWS ABQ confirms the seasonality independently: flash floods 'are most common during monsoon season (June 15 - September 30), particularly in July and August when all state areas can experience flooding.' This is the single largest consequence of the date change and the earlier research did not consider it.
monsoon.daily_pattern: Every authority that publishes a timing rule says the same thing: morning is safe, afternoon is not. NPS (Monsoon Season safety article): 'Finish hiking in the morning and be out of canyons or away from washes before the afternoon.' NWS Tucson monsoon safety: 'Plan outdoor activities to avoid being outside between mid afternoon and mid evening, especially in higher elevations where lightning is more common.' NPS White Sands: 'late afternoon and evening thunderstorms are common.' NPS Gila Cliff Dwellings (New Mexico mountains, same regime): powerful thunderstorms 'especially in the afternoons and evenings.' NO authority publishes an hour-by-hour climatology for the Sacramento Mountains themselves - that is recorded as unknown, not guessed. Two real NWS El Paso products for this exact drainage bracket the cycle in practice: a flood advisory logged 'At 236 PM MDT, Slow moving thunderstorms south of Cloudcroft have produced over an inch of rain south of Russia Canyon and near High Nogal', and a flash flood warning on the Rio Penasco was issued at 643 PM MDT and ran until 945 PM MDT. Working rule for the stay: walk and drive in the morning, be off the rim and out of every canyon bottom by early afternoon, and treat 14:00-21:00 as the storm window.
monsoon.lightning: Quantified where an authority publishes a figure, absent where none does. NWS Tucson: 'On average, over 1.5 million lightning strikes occur in Arizona and New Mexico each year. This accounts for over 15% of all lightning strikes in the lower 48 states.' NWS Albuquerque: 'lightning is the number one killer in New Mexico, with 84 deaths since 1959', and at least 78% of New Mexico lightning casualties occurred outdoors, in activities the page lists including hiking and biking. NPS: 'If you hear a clap of thunder, a thunderstorm is within 10 miles'; do not go back out 'for at least 30 minutes after the last thunder'. NWS Tucson: 'If fewer than 30 seconds elapse between the time you see a flash and hear the thunder, then the flash is less than 6 miles away.' NPS Gila, on the terrain that matters here: 'Avoid open ridges, exposed rock faces, and tall solitary trees.' NO strike-density figure is published for the Sacramento rim or for the White Sands dunefield - recorded as UNKNOWN. Practical read: the exposed 9,000 ft rim viewpoints and the bare gypsum dunefield are the two worst places to be caught, and both are the places the shot list wants you at.
monsoon.flash_flood: NWS Albuquerque, all direct quotes: 'Flash floods can occur with little or no warning, move at very fast speeds and can reach a peak in a few minutes.' 'Flash floods usually occur within six hours of heavy rainfall.' 'The varied terrain of New Mexico can channel water to locations that have not received rain.' 'Since 1959, 65 New Mexicans have lost their lives in flash floods' and 'It only takes about 1 to 2 feet of water to float most vehicles, including SUVs' (NWS Tucson) - 66 percent of those New Mexico deaths, 45 fatalities, 'occurred in a car'. NPS Gila states the mechanism that makes a canyon-bottom gravel road dangerous on a blue-sky afternoon: 'Even if skies are clear overhead, rainfall upstream can send a wall of water rushing down arroyos or trails with little warning.' The relevant hazard here is not being rained on. It is driving a canyon bottom while a storm sits over the headwaters where you cannot see it.
canyon_routes_affected: Upper Rio Penasco Road (County Road C17) - CONFIRMED FLASH-FLOOD CHANNEL, and this is the gravel ride the earlier research recommended. The Rio Penasco is named by NWS El Paso in warning text: a Flash Flood Warning for Central Otero County reads 'Earlier thunderstorms in the Mayhill area have caused flooding on the Rio Penasco. Due to the lack of gauges on this stream, it is difficult to know where the flooding currently is occurring, but it is most likely downstream (north and east) of the US-82 and Highway 130 corridor. With considerable runoff, it will take some time for stream levels to come down.' A separate NWS El Paso flood advisory (01 Aug 2026) tracks runoff 'towards Cox Canyon and the Rio Penasco'. Federal corroboration that this is a flood watershed by design: USDA NRCS built three flood-control dams here in 1959-60 - Bear Creek Dam, Curtis Canyon Dam and Graveyard Canyon Dam - whose 'original purpose ... was to provide flood protection for the Upper Penasco Watershed', and NRCS with the Otero Soil and Water Conservation District, the Forest Service and the Corps of Engineers are preparing a Supplemental Watershed Plan-Environmental Assessment for the Upper Rio Penasco (stakeholder notice dated 12 Mar 2026). CRITICAL: NWS says the stream is UNGAUGED. There is no river level to check before you go. The only usable signal is the forecast and the sky over the headwaters.

Water Canyon - NOT CONFIRMED EITHER WAY. No NWS product, Forest Service order or county notice naming Water Canyon as a flash-flood channel could be sourced. Neighbouring canyons in the same drainage system ARE named in NWS products - Cox Canyon, Russia Canyon, Wills Canyon, Agua Chiquita - so the absence is almost certainly a gap in what is published rather than evidence of safety. Recorded as UNKNOWN; treat as a canyon bottom under the same morning-only rule. This is a phone call to the Sacramento Ranger District.

Lincoln NF has closed ground on this district FOR monsoon flooding. Order 03-08-01-26-002, Area and Trails Closure, effective 02 Jun 2026, is stated as due to 'continued flooding effects through monsoon season and conditions have become hazardous'. That is the Forest Service itself confirming the mechanism on the Sacramento RD.

Separately and importantly for the offroad box: Order 03-08-02-25-001, effective 12 Aug 2025, closes four Sacramento RD areas - the RIO PENASCO, Bluff Springs, Wills Canyon and AGUA CHIQUITA - to dispersed camping, off-road motor vehicle use and campfires, cited for 'illegal off-highway vehicle use, resource damage to sensitive riparian areas, and ongoing restoration efforts'. A reported target end date of 31 Aug 2026 was described as subject to change and dependent on ecological recovery. Two of the routes in the existing card sit inside this closure. Status for 2029 is unknowable now and MUST be re-checked against the Lincoln NF alerts page before the stay.
monsoon.unpaved_roads_when_wet: The Forest Service says so on its own legal map. The Sacramento Ranger District Motor Vehicle Use Map (the MVUM, the legal document-of-record, downloaded from fs.usda.gov/media/241180) carries this text: 'Seasonal weather conditions and natural events may render designated roads and trails impassable for extended periods. Designated areas may contain dangerous or impassable terrain. Many designated roads and trails may be passable only by high-clearance vehicles or four-wheel-drive vehicles. Maintenance of designated roads and trails will depend on available resources, and many may receive little maintenance.' Per-road, only two are documented: FR 90 Westside Road - 'its middle section can be muddy, rutted, and extremely slippery when wet' (lincoln-nf-trails.org, a volunteer/partner trails site, NOT the Forest Service - flagged as such); and FR 63 to Lower Karr Canyon Campground, which the Forest Service's own district page says 'is gravel and can be rough'. Precedent that FS will shut a road outright on conditions alone: 'Road conditions have prompted an immediate road closure on the Sacramento Ranger District's La Luz Canyon Road (FS Road 00162 B)' (Lincoln NF official post). NO published wet-weather rating exists for FR 64, FR 24-series, Pumphouse, Agua Chiquita, Benson Ridge, Alamo Canyon or Three Mile Canyon - recorded as UNKNOWN, and it becomes a phone call. The truck is 4x4 and can handle mud; the exposure is being on the far side of a canyon crossing when it runs, not traction.
monsoon.white_sands: Monsoon impact is real and specific.07 in. Dunes Drive is 8 miles - the first 5 paved, the last 3 compacted gypsum sand, graded at least twice a week. NPS: 'During periods of heavy rain or snow, Dunes Drive will be very slick with water, snow, and/or ice, and visibility may be very poor', and when heavy rain is predicted 'the back half of Dunes Drive can become difficult to pass'. Wet gypsum is the specific hazard - the interdune flats hold water. The park may close all or part of Dunes Drive in heavy rain. MISSILE-TEST CLOSURES: no seasonal clustering is published by either NPS or WSMR, so the question 'do they cluster differently in August' is recorded as UNKNOWN rather than answered. What IS published: Dunes Drive 'may be closed for periods of up to three hours during military tests'; US-70 between Alamogordo and Las Cruces is closed at the same time; 'notifications from White Sands Missile Range may be received up to 24 hours in advance of a scheduled test'; the visitor center and gift shop stay open during closures. WSMR posts the roadblock schedule at wstc.army.mil/roadblocks.html, 'usually updated each weekday in the afternoon for the following day' - i.e. one day of notice, no long-range calendar. Phone for US-70 closures: 575-678-1178. Net effect on the plan: a White Sands day cannot be committed to more than 24 hours out, and since the reason to go in late August is the after-sunset window, an afternoon roadblock is survivable but a storm is not.

The 2026 edition is 29-30 August - road races Saturday 29th from 10:00 starting in Cloudcroft, gravel races Sunday 30th from 09:00 starting in High Rolls with a coordinated 08:30 descent from Cloudcroft. events.impact: Three ways it bites, and it is the most consequential event finding. (1) CAMPGROUND AVAILABILITY - a multi-course road and gravel event based in a village of this size will take lodging and sites; book the weekend nights early and re-check once the 2029 date is published. (2) ROADS - the courses use US-82, NM-130, NM-6563 the Sunspot Highway, Cathy Canyon, La Luz Canyon Road and Calico Peak Road, and finish at Upper Karr Canyon. Those are the same roads the scenic-drive box uses. Expect hundreds of cyclists on them for a morning, which argues for doing the Sunspot Highway drive on a different day. (3) It is also an opportunity - the one weekend the local gravel is marshalled, signed and has aid stations, and the shortest course, the 'Gravelina', is roughly a 10-mile out-and-back on Westside Road. Not a dog-in-a-carrier ride during a timed event, but it identifies Westside Road as the locally accepted easy gravel.

what_august_looks_like: Green, wet and stormy - not golden. The Forest Service describes the Sacramento Ranger District as mixed-conifer, 'ponderosa pine, Douglas fir, and aspen, along with stretches of pinon-juniper woodlands at lower elevations', with 'rolling pine-covered mountains, deep canyons, and expansive meadows', and places 'aspen groves turn vibrant gold' firmly in fall. So the aspen are green in late August and there is no colour to plan around. What replaces it is the monsoon green-up, and it is quantifiable: 5.65 in of rain falls in August against 0.88 in April and 1.31 in May (WRCC 291931). The meadows that are tan and dusty in June are green in late August, and the canyon bottoms - Rio Penasco, Agua Chiquita, Cox Canyon - are running rather than dry, which is the whole reason they are also dangerous. The real visual subject of a late-August stay is the weather itself: at 8,676 ft on the western rim you are looking DOWN on thunderstorms building over the Tularosa Basin and the White Sands dunefield, 4,000 ft below and an hour away, with virga, anvils and lightning over white gypsum in late-afternoon light. That is a better shot list than aspen and it exists only on these dates. CAUTION: no authority publishes a wildflower calendar for the Sacramento Mountains. Third-party trail listings claim 'summer brings wildflower blooms in the meadows' on trails such as the Osha Trail loop, but that is an unverified commercial listing and is recorded as such, not as a finding.
crowds: Busy, and this is the escape-the-desert peak. The Village of Cloudcroft says so itself: 'Each year, thousands of visitors escape the desert heat of southern New Mexico and Texas to experience Cloudcroft's cool alpine climate, scenic vistas, and endless outdoor adventures.' The arithmetic behind that is the temperature gap - Cloudcroft's August average maximum is 69.9 degF (WRCC) while El Paso and Las Cruces, both within easy day-trip range, are in the 90s and often triple digits; NPS gives White Sands summer daytime temperatures as 'often reach over 100 degF' and advises against hiking there above 85 degF. So the day-trip market from two cities is pointed straight at this village in late August, and summer is described by local guides as Cloudcroft's peak season. WEEKENDS ARE THE PRESSURE. Within the stay, Fri 24 - Sun 26 August is the exposed period, and if the Gran Fondo lands on 25-26 August in 2029 it will be the busiest weekend of the stay by a distance. Mon 27 and Tue 28 August should be the quietest days in the village - and they are also the two days the museum is shut, so they are the days to spend on the forest roads or at White Sands instead. Departing 29 August clears the Labor Day weekend crush entirely. No visitation figures are published for the village or the district, so 'busy' here is sourced qualitatively and by inference from the temperature gap, not counted. Practical consequence: the campground must be booked for the weekend nights specifically, and the booking re-confirmed once the Gran Fondo date for 2029 is published.

plan._why: The dates cannot move, so the constraints become a timetable rather than a reason to reschedule. Three things shape the week: the monsoon puts every canyon and forest-road outing in the MORNING; the museum opens Wed-Sat only; and the Gran Fondo takes US-82, the Sunspot Highway and La Luz Canyon Road on the last weekend of August, which is 25-26 Aug in 2029.

days.detail: US-82 up from Alamogordo is the hard part of the day — ~4,300 ft in 16-17 miles at a sustained 6% through the tunnel. Do it in the morning, before the storms build. Museum is open Wed 10:00-16:00, $5, if the drive goes quickly.

days.shape: White Sands, and the full moon works FOR you
days.detail: Full moon at 19:51 MDT. It kills the Milky Way for the week — but it is exactly what NPS runs its Full Moon Night for, May-Oct, when the park extends closing hours. The 22 May - 7 Sep extension is also in force, so the gate closes an hour after sunset rather than 30 minutes. Leashed dogs are legal on every trail and across the whole dunefield. This is the best single day of the stay.
Osha for the western rim and the view down onto the gypsum — frontlit in the morning, a silhouette by evening. Museum open. Village fills up through the day as Gran Fondo riders arrive.

days.shape: GRAN FONDO — stay off the highways
days.detail: The event uses US-82, the Sunspot Highway and La Luz Canyon Road. Not a day to drive the byway or ride the shoulder. Village walking, the Trestle Recreation Area, and the museum, which is open.
Museum shut Sun-Tue. Event traffic clearing. Short trails from camp in the morning.

days.shape: GRAVEL RIDE — early start, canyon out by noon
days.detail: Upper Rio Penasco with the dog in the carrier. This is the day with the least traffic on it, and the ride has to be a morning ride: the Rio Penasco is a flash-flood channel with no stream gauge, so there is nothing to check before setting off. Out of the canyon before early afternoon.
Down US-82 in the morning for the same reason you came up it in one. Departing on the 29th clears the Labor Day weekend crush entirely.
